title: What are the top new games of Gamescom 2026?
text:

What are the top new games of Gamescom 2026?
We look at GDCo Pro’s wishlist leaderboards. Also: new GameDiscoverCo Show & lotsa news..
Simon Carless
Sep 02, 2026
[The GameDiscoverCo game discovery newsletter is written by ‘how people find your game’ expert & company founder Simon Carless, and is a regular look at how people discover and buy video games in the 2020s.]
Welcome back from Gamescom, for those who gaily attended, and it’s all uphill (downhill?) until the end of the year from here. But we all have a few video games to launch and monitor in the meantime. Let’s get to it…
Before we start, we can’t be the only ones low-key obsessed with the McDonalds UK x Xbox special food menu ? Specifically, there’s spicy chicken nuggets ‘inspired by’ the Moa bird in Halo, and, uhh, “Blamco Cheese Bites inspired by Fallout 76’s™ Blamco Mac & Cheese.” You can also “engage with content” and unlock in-game items . Synergy, folks!
[ NEED THE BEST DATA? You can get a free demo of our GameDiscoverCo Pro company-wide ‘Steam deep dive’ & console data, inc. MCP server, by reaching out today - >110 orgs have it. Or, signing up to GDCo Plus gets extra newsletter and Discord access, plus more .]
Game disco news: PS5 gets... ad-supported TV?
Let’s kick things off for the week with a whole mess of game platform & discovery news, as follows:
There’s a new Steam data leak from earlier in the platform’s history . The “so-called ‘teraleak’ contains over 12 terabytes of file depots served through Steam from 2003 to 2013” , including early builds of Valve games (Portal, Left 4 Dead, Dota 2), but also third-party titles with private Steam builds. (Misconfigured endpoint leak?)
An unexpected launch on PlayStation would be ‘Live TV on PS5’, which offers “a free ad-supported experience from Sony Pictures Television” in the U.S., including movies (a 50 Cent-themed action channel!), TV shows (Community, The Walking Dead), anime (Naruto, Death Note, exclusive Crunchyroll channels) & more.
After signaling it would, Xbox is cutting out other platforms from trailers on the Xbox YouTube channel , with no mentions of the non-Xbox SKUs for Minecraft Dungeons II. (The full platform list is on other versions, but the fans are sated…)
Gamescom 2026 was, in general, a hit with attendees, with 368k (non-unique) visitors from 131 countries & 1,743 (!) exhibitors. (The organizers might have done a tad better responding to indie dev/publishers laptop thefts tho, since their literal ‘let’s tell you about the regulations’ response was seen as non-sympathetic.)
We talk about console hardware price hikes, but how about PC? PC Gamer helps us understand : “B efore the memory crisis, there was quite an abundance of RTX 5060 gaming PCs… [as low as] $749… these days you're looking at almost $1,000 for the same thing , and that's if you're lucky.” (PCs can be upgraded more modularly, but..)
Valve was chatting to devs at Gamescom, and Yaroslav Shalashov passes along two tidbits : “Steam Networking will support crossplay, and you'll be able to build multiplayer for [console/other] platforms on a single system.” Also: “the Steam game analytics section [inc. the] median time metric will be reworked” , hopefully by EOY?
PlayStation things: ahead of the GTA VI launch, “PS5 Pro is currently sold out across [U.S.] retailers online … it’s still available on PS Direct or at significant markups ($1,200+) from third party sellers” ; State Of Play showcase is back on Thursday Sept. 3rd , inc. first & third-party games (and a warning about licensed music for co-streaming.)
Not the cheeriest, but Kim Nordstrom’s post-Gamescom trend commentary is worth a peek: “Early Access looks pretty broken on PC… Ship a solid core loop immediately, or focus on quality with AA.” But here’s a plus: “Our global TAM is only 3.5B of 8.3B alive - 4B in a few years, maybe 5B in a decade-ish.” Number… go up?
Former Gamefam founder/firebrand Joe Ferencz has opinions about Roblox’s algo changes to prioritize ‘highly retentive games’ vs. meme-y hits: “[Roblox] is a company looking at the greatest hit factory in the history of interactive entertainment and deciding the hits are the problem. The hits are not the problem. The hits are the product.”
One thing that we missed in that BBC x Xbox Asha Sharma interview last week that The Verge picked up on : “We’ve been hard at work on a great next generation and a great family of devices for Helix, and we’ll share more soon.” Family of devices, huh? (Perhaps both first and third party-made ones, rather than multiple first-party?)
OUR SPONSOR: FirstLook Analytics + Engagement
You can see your wishlist count. You can’t see who’s behind it. FirstLook just launched Analytics + Engagement . Pins every session, retention cohort, playtime figure and custom event to the actual player who generated it, in-game and out.
Build a segment: five-plus sessions, back on day seven, five-star survey. It fills itself as players qualify. Then let it fire the beta key wave on its own, or ask the FirstLook agent to build the whole journey for you.
Free up to 100,000 player profiles, with free Unreal and Unity SDKs. Paid plans from $99/month: Request a demo .
What are the top new games of Gamescom 2026?
The top titles from Opening Night Live, and wishlist percentiles…
Like us, you’ve probably been tracking the many titles that got promoted in multiple ways (show floor, creator outreach, streaming showcases) at Gamescom 2026 in Germany last week. And thanks to GDCo Pro ’s new Streaming Showcase Tracker (above, for ONL), we’re monitoring the Steam side of things in impeccable detail.
Here’s the streaming showcases we were monitoring last week, with an important caveat - some (with a *) haven’t reached the ‘7 day’ limit we compare wishlists against, so their numbers will still go up. Nonetheless, here’s the general direction of travel:
Note: we do include ‘pre-show highlighted games’ in these numbers, which increases the # of games for multiple showcases (depending on how you classify!)
You may not be surprised to see Gamescom’s official Geoff Keighley-collab-ing Opening Night Live 2026 as the leading showcase. (It actually has >5x median wishlist increases than any other showcase.) So we’ll initially concentrate on that showcase’s charts, to see what made a big splash. Here’s the Top 15 games, by 7 day wishlist gain:
(All of these wishlist balance increases are GDCo estimates - they’ll be indicative, but non-perfect.)
You can see a variety of titles crowding in here, including some very close to release, and also a bunch of new games. Some notes on them:
New takes on existing IP were two of the top three games: Wizards Of The Coast’s new third-person ARPG using the D&D license, Warlock , came out at #1 (+375k wishlists) , and a double-IP game - Lego x existing city-builder Cities Skylines, in LEGO Skylines - also got a ton of interest at #2 (+315k WLs) .
A strong showing for Asian devs is topped by Ananta : the anime open-world RPG published by NetEase hit #3 with +350k wishlists, and other strong AAA-looking titles from Asia include Arthurian ARPG Tides Of Annihilation (#11) and F2P creature-catcher Aniimo (#12) . (There’s also two MiHoYo games, Nodusfall & Petit Planet, that aren’t going onto Steam soon, but have lots of interest.)
The rest of the Top 10 has a fascinating mix of new & existing IP: there’s a rejigger of a hot old PC franchise ( Heroes Of Might & Magic III Remake , +210k WLs) , first-person cyberpunk-er No Law (+160k WLs) , Paradox’s post-apoc grand strategy game Afterworld (+150k), and upcoming Metro & Rainbow Six titles.
If there’s a ‘feel’ across these titles, btw, there’s a lot of deeper, grittier titles in a variety of genres. To us: (non-cute) fantasy, post-apocalypse, cyberpunk, and distressed, ‘lived in’ worlds are in. (With some anime-ish & Lego exceptions, we’re not seeing bright, happy aesthetics in these charts. Every day is like Sunday , rite?)
BTW, it’s very notable that 65 of the 72 games mentioned in any way in Opening Night live had a Steam page at that point. (The only ones not: Worms, Nodusfall, 1001 Threads Of Mizan, Silver Palace, Monster Hunter Outlanders (mobile), Petit Planet, and Zoopunk, and >50% of these will get Steam pages in due course.)
Next, let’s look briefly at just the debuts we spotted in Opening Night Live. We see 17 of the top 50 announces in there that were (basically) brand new for the showcase:
We’ve already talked about a bunch of the Top 15-ranked, but there’s a ton of other interesting titles lower down: top-down ARPG Tarae: The Unbound , the Starship Troopers-y Exterminauts , fascinating-looking puzzle adventure Lofsong , roguelite PUBG expansion DED.NET , a new Rollercoaster Tycoon game , and more.
Since a lot of these games were blitzing Gamescom, they often appeared in multiple of the showcases - as well as talking to the press & sometimes on the show floor. And reminder: we don’t try to separate wishlist increases by showcase . (We’re just showing wishlists in the 7 days after the showcase, no matter how they turned up…)
Anyhow, a quick audit of the other showcases reveals a few uniques: the kinda adorable raccoon co-op-er Dumpster Gang and strategy/tower defense sequel Kingdom III: Rising Realms both added 50-70k wishlists while appearing in the longform 2-day Xbox showcase . (More like a magazine program, less of a trailerfest!)
But the Future Games Show @ Gamescom was more traditionally trailer-y, and in addition to overlap even with Xbox, showed unique games like hack & slasher Wolcen 2 and cozy tavern sim D&D: Long Rest Tavern , both of which started nicely with at least 50k more Steam wishlists. And that’s the shape of Gamescom - congrats, all…
GameDiscoverCo Show: Valve’s 30 years, checked
Last but not least, we’re back with The GameDiscover Show , ft. myself (Simon) and Post Games’ Chris Plante zipping through the stories of the week - sub to the podcast via Apple Music , Spotify & elsewhere (audio), with a video version on YouTube (above).
On this episode , we talk about Valve's 30 year anniversary and the inexorable (?) rise of Steam as a platform, ruminate on Battle.net getting third-party game additions with The Witcher 3, examine a change to more personalized midweek deals on Steam, and discuss how hit PC game genres have changed since 2021. Check it…
[ We’re GameDiscoverCo , an analysis firm based around one simple issue: how do players find, buy and enjoy your PC or console game? We run the newsletter you’re reading, and provide real-time data services for publishers, funds, and other smart game industry folks.]

title: Roblox’s Expensive Year of Good Intentions
text:
Roblox lost nearly a third of its value after reporting its Q2 2026 results at the end of July. The stock now trades near $37, about 75% below its 2025 peak and well below its listing price from five years ago. Around $70B in market value has evaporated over the past twelve months.

Roblox's business did not fall as heavily. In Q2, revenue grew 36% and daily active users (DAU) grew 10% YoY. Quarter over quarter, revenue is flat while DAU is declining.

Roblox stock price
Source: Naavik analysis
Roblox had an extraordinary 2025, and the market priced it for more of the same. So, it turns out, did management. That makes this an expectations reset more than a business failure. It is not only an expectations problem: Roblox was already cooling as it began making changes that added even more pressure on growth and monetization. The more interesting question is whether those changes are temporary self-inflicted pain or whether they are landing on top of a business that was slowing anyway.

Look at Bookings, Not Revenue
Roblox's reported revenue is a lagging indicator. When someone buys Robux, that money is recognized as revenue gradually over the estimated lifetime of a paying user (27 months at the company’s last disclosure). This makes the 36% YoY revenue growth an echo of last year's boom. Bookings, which capture the sale when the Robux is purchased, are the number that tells you what is happening right now.

Roblox Revenue
Source: Roblox and Naavik analysis
Bookings grew 8% in Q2 year over year but declined quarter over quarter. The quarterly numbers are where the predicament shows up: DAU has declined for three consecutive quarters, bookings for two, and monthly unique payers have fallen alongside them. Spending per user fell too, with bookings per daily user down 2% YoY and bookings per payer down 6%. Fewer players, each spending a little less.

Three things stand out:

The decline predates the algorithm change. DAU peaked in Q3 2025 and bookings in Q4. April's discovery update landed on a platform that was already cooling.
Roblox is doing the worst where the money is. U.S. and Canada are the best-monetizing markets, and bookings there stayed essentially flat YoY. Meanwhile, Europe grew by 18%, Asia-Pacific by 14%, and the rest of the world by 31%.
The outlook is worse than the quarter. Roblox withdrew its full-year outlook and guided Q3 to a revenue growth of 4–10% and a bookings decline of 14–18%. It's the first bookings decline the company has ever guided to, and the main reason the stock crashed.
Some of the Pain is Self-Inflicted
A number of the biggest headwinds are the result of choices management made deliberately. That does not make them good choices: the case rests on whether today’s lost growth buys Roblox a stronger platform later.

The business is maturing. Nothing grows 20% a year forever. Roblox's stated ambition is 10% of global gaming content revenue. It currently has less than 4% of that market. That is both an enormous business and a long way from the target. The goal was always going to get harder as the base got bigger.

2025 was a spike, not a slope. Grow a Garden and the brainrot wave that followed it broke concurrent-player records and monetized far above anything Roblox could reasonably expect to repeat. Entertainment is hit-driven, and platforms are no exception. Developers keep getting better (and of course, there is even Grow a Garden 2 now), but you cannot commission lightning. Sustaining 70% growth was never realistic.

Safety adds friction. Age checks became mandatory for chat in January. It’s very much defensible, but it does put an extra step between a new user and the social interaction that Roblox is really about. Verification also shrank the adult audience on paper: the share of players Roblox counts as 18+ was lower once ages were verified rather than self-reported.

Discovery now optimizes for retention. Roblox expanded its Recommended For You algorithm from a 7-day view to a 28-day view, with separate signals for Day 1, Days 2–7, and Days 8–28. Roblox is deliberately sending fewer players toward the experiences that monetized hardest, and it says the effect on under-13 spending in North America was bigger than expected.

Both discovery and safety are better understood as investments than as headwinds.

Investing in safety is the clearest case. Right now, it is friction and legal expense. But in the long run, regulation is a tax on Roblox and a barrier to everyone smaller. It is also a precondition for the advertising business because you cannot sell targeted inventory against an audience whose ages you do not know.

Engagement-weighted discovery has precedent. YouTube famously shifted from clicks to watch time in 2012, and Google later applied similar thinking to Google Play. Early on, a UGC platform needs supply: more creators, more content, more reasons to open the app. Eventually, a successful platform drowns in content, and the real job becomes deciding what deserves an audience. This is what Roblox is now trying to solve, and what YouTube, Steam, the App Store, and Google Play all went through.

Roblox's platform is unusually vertically integrated. It owns discovery, payments, hosting, identity, and currency. Changing discovery redistributes income across an entire economy, which is why developers spent April watching their impressions move and arguing about whether it was a bug or the point. The question is subtler than "the algorithm hurt me." If distribution now depends on 28-day retention, how does a brand-new game ever prove it has any?

It also makes Roblox game studios harder to invest in or buy. Anyone writing a check wants to know what a game will earn next year, and that guess assumes traffic keeps behaving as it did last year. Roblox has to keep changing discovery, but predictability is worth something too.

A standalone publisher can survive a bad recommendation algorithm by getting traffic elsewhere. A Roblox developer has far fewer places to go. The healthier Roblox makes discovery for players, the more consequential (and potentially frustrating) its decisions become for creators.

The Long-Term Bet
Roblox’s bet is this: the company is deliberately accepting a worse 2026 in the hope that 2028 is better. The problem is that not all of 2026’s weakness was deliberate.

The good case is still compelling. Retention-focused discovery produces better games, safety changes make the platform easier to regulate and monetize, older users deepen the audience, and DAU growth resumes once the transition settles. Bookings recover.

The bad case is simpler. Roblox gets through the discovery transition and absorbs the safety friction, but growth still does not pick up; Roblox will have given up near-term bookings for nothing.

That is why the guidance misses matter. In February, Roblox told investors to expect 22–26% bookings growth in 2026. In April, it cut that to 8–12%. In July, it withdrew the outlook and guided Q3 to a decline. Naveen Chopra took over as CFO in mid-2025, so the February number was his first annual guide, and it lasted a single quarter.

Some of this is genuinely unforecastable, but not all of it. Roblox set that February number knowing its own age checks and its own algorithm change were coming, and misjudged both. Netflix spent years learning to guide a business it couldn't fully predict, and got good at it. Roblox has to do the same: test the changes before promising the results. Right now, management may be right about the destination, but it hasn’t shown it can price the trip.

Getting through the transition is only half the problem. Roblox still needs credible sources for future growth. Part of the answer is simple. Roblox needs more breakout hits. The 2025 surge came from content, and the next surge will too. What Roblox controls is whether the platform makes hits more likely: better tools, discovery that finds them early, and economics that keep the studios capable of building them. 

The other part is aging up. Adults are 27% of age-checked daily users, and U.S. users over 18 monetize over 50% better than users under 18. Roblox now pays creators roughly 42% more on qualifying spend from age-checked American adults, a direct attempt to buy that content into existence. If bookings per user are going to rise without squeezing children harder, older players are the answer.

The question is whether Roblox understands what it needs to do to get them. Investor communications have leaned for two years on high-fidelity, AAA-grade experiences as the route to that audience, as though what keeps adults away were the graphics.

Roblox Build
Roblox Build | Source: Roblox
The stronger argument is that older players want depth: persistent economies, progression that compounds, strategy, social competition, real cooperation. None of that needs AAA graphics, and most of it plays to what Roblox already is. The worst outcome is a console game trapped inside Roblox: more expensive than a Roblox game, worse than a real one.

Successful Roblox games already work like well-run mobile games: a steady drip of new content, rewards for logging in each day, seasonal challenges you pay to unlock, and carefully balanced in-game currencies. A discovery system that now rewards month-long retention only pushes developers further that way.

Roblox does not need to build those games itself. Nobody else in UGC gaming has a network this size, and nobody else can spend against it the way Roblox can. That advantage is real and it is not going away this year. With the newly introduced Build, Roblox is showing where a chunk of that spending goes: prompt-to-game creation inside the mobile app and agents in Studio for playtesting, analytics, and experiments. Developers have been lukewarm on in-engine AI assistants elsewhere, but Roblox might be better positioned than any other company to make it work. The bigger opportunity, though, is in the boring stuff done right: development and publishing tooling, analytics, moderation, discovery creators can plan around, and safety they inherit for free. This is what decides whether the next hit gets built here.

Investors now have to distinguish patience from excuses. The likeliest path is neither collapse nor a fast rebound; it’s a few more quarters of growing pains while the transition works through, and a company that comes out of it bigger than the one that went in.

title: Hearth & Hamlet’s ~100k & the rise of the bite-sized clicker...
text:
Hearth & Hamlet’s ~100k & the rise of the bite-sized clicker...
Also: news news news, and Steam’s new games this week
Simon Carless
Aug 29, 2026
∙ Paid
[The GameDiscoverCo game discovery newsletter is written by ‘how people find your game’ expert & company founder Simon Carless, and is a regular look at how people discover and buy video games in the 2020s.]
Welcome to ‘the tail end of Gamescom week’, and yep, it’s busy for new game reveals: GameFile rounded up the high-profile Opening Night Live handily , and you should also peep Future Games Show’s line-up , the Xbox Games Showcase Pt. 1 and Pt.2 , and more. (We’ll have more on this next week, for those obsessed with who did the best.)
And before we finish up with Gamescom, a million points to whoever designed the ARC Raiders show-floor booth for Embark - apparently you’re running around it like you’re inside the game? Sounds like more fun than staring at monitors, to us…
[ HAVEN’T CHECKED PRO YET? You can get a free demo of our GameDiscoverCo Pro company-wide ‘Steam deep dive’ & console data, inc. MCP by reaching out today - >110 orgs have it. Or, signing up to GDCo Plus gets extra newsletter and Discord access, plus more.]
Game discovery news: Onimusha’s demo goes big
So, let’s take a look at the latest game discovery & platform news, which appears to be the following:
GDCo Pro’s top Steam demos for unreleased games (above) is headed by an expanded demo for Capcom's much-anticipated Onimusha: Way Of The Sword, then continued hits Guildrun (#2) & Nomad Drive (#3). (Two massive Betas, for CoD: Modern Warfare 4 (115k CCU) and for Wardogs (106k CCU) also happened...)
Xbox things: the ‘ physical disc to digital item’ program is here , testable by Xbox Insiders on Aug. 31st; Windows Central has some more details , inc. that most (tho not all) Xbox Series & Xbox One discs are compatible; Asha Sharma chatted to the BBC that Xbox needs to be "thinking about" affordability for its next console.
About that ‘Battle.net getting more third-party games’ rumor? Blizzard just announced a collab with CD Projekt to bring The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered to the PC platform, as well as “gain access to a Geralt-themed skin in Diablo IV” if you buy it on there. (It’s like the ‘Fortnite skins’ move on EGS…)
Steam has an archive of their latest Next Fest video Q&A , with Ria Hu saying re: common dev mistakes: “People rush so much to get everything in order for Next Fest that they don’t have or… take the time to step back and say, ‘Okay, what am I really presenting to customers?’” ( Getting a third party to poke at your store page is key.)
We’re also publishing GDCo Twitch game chart analysis onto LinkedIn , and top games watched (released in last 6 months, 7 days to Aug 28th!) include Souls-like Mortal Shell II, fish&gun friendslopper How To Fish and basketball game NBA 2K27 as the only new games with >2m hours watched, last 7 days. ( More within ..)
Microlinks: PlayStation Plus’ monthly games for September inc. Sniper Elite: Resistance, MLB The Show 26, and Wobbly Life; Google talks about its 15 years of AI research in games (inc. EVE Online newness); some rare data on micro-indies being ported to console ($15k console rev. for a racer, $3-4k for smaller games.)
Discord’s doing more in-depth collabs , inc. Play Quest+ with Battlefield 6, where “players who accept the Quest and link their Discord and EA accounts can complete a gameplay objective to unlock rewards”, while “progress is automatically updated in Discord as users play.” (Also: Bloons TD6 and Rust items buyable direct in Discord.)
Y’know how console manufacturers are getting U.S. tariff refunds but don’t intend to refund buyers ? Well, buyers of Panic’s Playdate handheld are getting $ back , aided by all Playdates being bought D2C (easier refund tracking…) Refunding $12.36 “felt like the fair thing to do”, says Panic. (Much respect.)
Two mini-updates on previous stories: looks like EA pulled its digital data from Circana (after going private) at the same time Xbox did; and ‘shovelware-adjacent’ PlayStation publisher Ternox (of STONKS-9800 fame) had its publisher access restored , after Sony evidently decided it was on the right side of the line.
Aftermath has been speaking to some indies about Steam’s relatively opaque adult content eval pipeline : “For [ Perfect Tides: Station To Station dev Meredeith] Gran, after she submitted her build full of the sex scenes, Steam took ‘probably about two weeks’ to get back to her, during which she was ‘sweating.’”
Microlinks, Pt. 2: talking of tariffs, the Trump admin is looking at new U.S. semi-conductor tariffs that could include game consoles ; mobile D2C (App Store cut-avoiding) $ got big, with 20-50% off-platform for some firms ; Fields Of Mistria players really want polyamory in the game , per a fun Discord server analysis.

All self-serve, all free to use.
Whether you’re prepping a launch or already shipping, get started at indie.io/start .
Hearth & Hamlet’s ~100k & the rise of the bite-sized clicker...
You may have noticed us covering more <$10 games, often by solo or tiny devs, on GDCo recently. Why? It’s mainly because were ‘following the players’, and a notably large percentage of these turn up in our top new games of the week on Steam by CCU.
One trend we’ve definitely noticed is the rise of the incremental genre which - to quote Wikipedia , is “ a video game subgenre characterized by the incremental accumulation of in-game resources, and gradual, often exponential progression through repetitive actions or automation.” Two recent things made us look further at the space.
Firstly, HTMAG has some great mini-profiles on recent indie incremental hits in different genres, inc. on Sir, We Have An Orc Problem ($10, 4 month dev, 230k units est., incremental tower defense w/huge # of enemies) & on Bills Must Be Paid ($7, 7 month dev, 420k units est., incremental piggie bank-smashin’!)
And secondly, Polden’s Kirill Oreshkin singled out incremental games as a major new trend on Steam , saying: “ I decided to research some incremental [PC] games I hadn’t played before…. Holy shit…You can’t stop playing. You’re hooked immediately.” (He calls them ‘hypercasual’, which is another possible name for this genre on PC…)
Anyhow, before we draw more conclusions, we have one particular game to analyze - Phorust Studios & Runic Forge’s Hearth & Hamlet ($8), “a medieval citybuilder clicker that blends resource management, in-depth upgrade trees and relaxing idle gameplay.” Aidan McGrath at Rune was kind enough to provide us current stats for the 9-day old game:
That’s pretty darn good for a title made by a solo dev from Australia, who works a dayjob as a teacher. We imagine it’ll gross >$2m in the medium term? Other key points around the game:
Aidan tells us that “the game actually started as a fun incremental for [the dev’s] class at school to play” , and its biggest inspirations are Cast N Chill (for vibes), Ropuka’s Idle Island , Microcivilization and Tower Wizard .
Median playtime of 7 hours 20 minutes is spectacular, given it’s so early in the game’s lifecycle & the game takes 8-12 hours to complete in total…
Regionally, the U.S. is 23% of the units, followed by China (14.5%), Germany (13%), Japan (6%), Korea (5%), the UK, Canada, and Taiwan (4%), and down from there. (Having a regional sub-publisher , Gamersky, probably helped in Asia..)
And there’s a wider point, as Aidan from Rune explained to us: “We’ve seen a shift towards incrementals that are more ‘active’ - where, rather than idling , players are actually playing the game .” This has been the revelation to me - that a lot of incremental games are highly distilled, strong game-loop ‘number go up’ takes on specific genres.
(Although H&H is a clicker, you can hold doing the button and there’s now a ‘Hover to Click’ feature - so… it’s about ‘number go up’, not clicking.)
Hearth & Hamlet is an interesting case. If you look at the above screenshot, you might think you design the paths and place the buildings by hand. But as the dev explains : “The city layout is completely predetermined. Think of it as assembling a pre-designed diorama. This is intentional as it is designed as a more relaxing incremental approach.”
Rune’s McGrath agrees that this “led to some weird expectations.... a substantial portion of our negative reviews are specifically non-idle players, who wanted a stronger city-builder experience.” But we think the game picked up a lot of attention due to its looks & playability, and it’s hanging at 79% Positive Steam user reviews, which ain’t shabby.
Oh, and a bonus, since everyone loves annotated wishlist graphs? The game hit >200k Steam wishlists by launch, aided by a popular demo, and here’s the rundown, per Rune
So, some conclusions: the rise of the LitRPG as a book genre proves that today’s ‘media consumers’ love progression as a key part of their experience. And we think the promise of these incremental games - sub-$10 price, strong hook, a blessedly finite experience - are a big win for players plagued with a backlog of 50-hour long games.
Another key point is low(er) barriers to entry. I liked Kirill Oreshkin’s take on this : “ You sit down to play, a… tutorial begins, and your brain goes: ‘Aaaaargh! Effort! Don’t want effort! Want to play! Don’t want to learn!’ Sometimes you’re simply out of energy and looking for rest in a game.” Maybe games like this are… what many players actually want?
This week on Steam: Zero Company, MGS do gud!
